title: The Gulf Isn’t Ready for a Renewed Iran War
gist: Handjani argues that robust Gulf oil flow figures (24m b/d via Hormuz and bypasses vs 23.3m prewar) mask years-long physical damage to refineries, LNG trains and terminals from eight months of Iran war. A renewed post-midterm U.S.-Israeli campaign would hit depleted air defenses and both Saudi export routes, risking permanent market-share loss for Gulf producers; a negotiated settlement mediated by Qatar is the cheaper path.

insights.claim: Oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and alternative routes averaged more than 24 million barrels a day in the week ending Oct. 18, 2026, above the prewar level of 23.3 million, according to Kpler.
insights.speaker: Amir Handjani
insights.so_what: Headline flow data looks reassuring and may be lulling markets into underpricing supply risk.
insights.locator: By the narrow measure of barrels

insights.claim: JPMorgan analysts say energy markets are 'converging on a forever conflict,' a view that has encouraged the Trump administration to believe the Gulf can absorb another round of fighting.
insights.speaker: Amir Handjani
insights.so_what: Sell-side complacency is feeding policy risk-taking, a reflexive loop that raises tail risk.
insights.quote: energy markets are “converging on a forever conflict”
insights.locator: By the narrow measure of barrels

insights.claim: The author contends that judging Gulf resilience by barrels shipped confuses current flow with the deteriorating state of the plants and terminals that move the oil and gas, much of which will take years to rebuild.
insights.speaker: Amir Handjani
insights.so_what: Spare capacity and resilience buffers are thinner than volumes suggest, so the next shock could have outsized price impact.
insights.quote: That view confuses how much oil and gas are still flowing from the Gulf with the state of the plants and terminals that move it.
insights.locator: That view confuses how much oil

insights.claim: A Reuters investigation documented at least 135 Iranian drone and missile attacks on at least 84 infrastructure sites across seven Gulf states since the war began on Feb. 28, 2026.
insights.speaker: Amir Handjani
insights.so_what: Breadth of damage across the Gulf asset base implies a broad, not isolated, capacity impairment.
insights.quote: at least 135 Iranian drone and missile attacks on at least 84 infrastructure sites across seven Gulf states

insights.claim: Iranian-linked strikes have damaged five of Saudi Arabia's nine largest refineries and both export manifolds at Fujairah, the UAE's main terminal outside Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Amir Handjani
insights.so_what: Refined product supply and Hormuz-bypass export capacity are both impaired, supporting product cracks.
insights.quote: damaged five of Saudi Arabia’s nine largest refineries and both export manifolds at Fujairah

insights.claim: Strikes on cold boxes at Qatar's Ras Laffan took out two LNG trains representing about 17% of Qatar's export capacity, with QatarEnergy expecting three to five years of repairs and an estimated $20 billion in lost annual revenue.
insights.speaker: Amir Handjani
insights.so_what: A multi-year structural hole in global LNG supply favors non-Gulf LNG exporters and supports long-dated LNG prices.
insights.quote: took out two LNG trains representing about 17 percent of Qatar’s export capacity

insights.claim: Because much of the damaged Gulf energy equipment is custom-built, the supply losses will outlast any cease-fire or peace agreement with Iran.
insights.speaker: Amir Handjani
insights.so_what: Peace headlines would not quickly restore lost capacity; don't assume a fast normalization trade.
insights.quote: Since much of this equipment is custom-built, the losses will outlast any cease-fire or peace agreement with Iran.

insights.claim: The UAE reported intercepting 132 of 137 ballistic missiles on the war's first day, and JINSA estimated more than 90% of Iranian projectiles were intercepted theater-wide by March.
insights.speaker: Amir Handjani
insights.so_what: Strong air-defense stats underpin the case for a renewed campaign but are the wrong risk metric for energy assets.

insights.claim: The author's framework: energy infrastructure risk depends not on the share of missiles stopped but on what the few that get through hit, since a refinery or LNG complex goes offline after losing a single critical component.
insights.speaker: Amir Handjani
insights.so_what: Single-point-of-failure exposure means even high interception rates leave large tail risk to supply.
insights.quote: A refinery or LNG complex does not need to be hit repeatedly to be taken offline; it needs to lose only one critical component.

insights.claim: Qatar intercepted four of five ballistic missiles Iran fired at Ras Laffan on March 18, yet that 80% interception rate still produced years-long LNG supply loss; the FT reported the missiles were maneuverable enough to evade Patriot batteries.
insights.speaker: Amir Handjani
insights.so_what: Illustrates that Gulf energy assets are vulnerable even under successful defense.
insights.quote: An 80 percent interception rate still produced a loss of LNG supply that will last for years.

insights.claim: JINSA estimated that by late March Bahrain had used up to 87% of its Patriot interceptors and the UAE and Kuwait roughly 75%, so a second round would start from a weaker defensive position.
insights.speaker: Amir Handjani
insights.so_what: Interceptor depletion raises the odds of successful hits in a renewed war and supports demand for missile-defense production.
insights.locator: A second round would also begin

themes.theme: Houthi Red Sea front and Saudi bypass vulnerability

insights.claim: Since declaring a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia on July 20, the Houthis have struck Saudi Aramco's 400,000 b/d Jizan refinery three times, forcing it offline in August.
insights.speaker: Amir Handjani
insights.so_what: Saudi refining is under attack from a second front independent of Iran.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, since declaring a naval blockade

insights.claim: Drone strikes on the East-West pipeline in September forced Riyadh to shut it for 11 days, halting Yanbu loadings, making the Hormuz bypass one of the most exposed parts of the Saudi export system.
insights.speaker: Amir Handjani
insights.so_what: The key Hormuz contingency route is itself unreliable, raising the risk of simultaneous loss of both Saudi export outlets.
insights.quote: The pipeline built to cope with a Hormuz closure has become one of the most exposed parts of the Saudi export system.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, since declaring a naval blockade

insights.claim: Iranian strikes on Saudi oil facilities combined with the Houthi campaign would put both Saudi export routes under simultaneous attack, lengthening recovery timelines toward a decade and eroding the Saudi spare capacity that has absorbed supply shocks since the 1990s.
insights.speaker: Amir Handjani
insights.so_what: Loss of OPEC spare capacity would structurally raise oil volatility and risk premia.
insights.quote: Recovery timelines would lengthen toward a decade, and the Saudi spare capacity that has absorbed supply shocks since the 1990s would erode.
insights.locator: Iranian strikes on Saudi oil facilities

themes.theme: Importer pain in Asia and Europe

insights.claim: Asia, which received nearly nine-tenths of Hormuz crude before the war, has borne the brunt: Bangladesh rationed fuel and diverted gas from four of five state fertilizer plants, Pakistan imposed a four-day workweek, India capped households at one subsidized cooking-gas cylinder every 25 days, and the Philippines declared a national energy emergency.
insights.speaker: Amir Handjani
insights.so_what: Energy-importing EMs face growth, fiscal and fertilizer/food-security stress; watch EM FX and sovereign spreads.

insights.claim: By September, Bangladeshi garment exporters reported canceled orders and idled lines, and rotating blackouts in May left nearly 2 million people on Luzon without power.
insights.speaker: Amir Handjani
insights.so_what: Energy shortages are spilling into manufacturing and export supply chains such as apparel.

insights.claim: Europe's exposure runs mainly through refined products, with European diesel premiums hitting records in September 2026.
insights.speaker: Amir Handjani
insights.so_what: Middle-distillate tightness is the European transmission channel; diesel cracks are a key watch item.
insights.quote: Europe’s exposure runs mainly through refined products; European diesel premiums hit records in September.

themes.theme: Permanent market-share shift away from the Gulf

insights.claim: On Oct. 22, QatarEnergy signed a deal to buy up to 4 million metric tons a year of U.S. LNG from Cheniere through 2054, supply that does not pass through Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Amir Handjani
insights.so_what: Even Gulf producers are hedging with U.S. LNG, a long-duration tailwind for U.S. LNG exporters.
insights.locator: Iranian strikes on Saudi oil facilities

insights.claim: If fighting resumes, Gulf producers may find that market share ceded to the United States, to coal and to other suppliers does not return, as buyers' adjustments become permanent.
insights.speaker: Amir Handjani
insights.so_what: Structural winners include U.S. energy exporters and coal; Gulf NOCs face lasting share loss.
insights.quote: Gulf producers may find that the market share they cede to the United States, to coal, and to other suppliers does not return.
insights.locator: Iranian strikes on Saudi oil facilities

insights.claim: The Gulf's reputation as a dependable supplier rested on decades of redundancy investment premised on U.S. power deterring attacks, an assumption this year's fighting has overturned.
insights.speaker: Amir Handjani
insights.so_what: A structural repricing of Gulf supply reliability argues for higher risk premia and diversification by importers.
insights.quote: This year’s fighting has overturned that assumption.
insights.locator: The Gulf’s reputation as a dependable

insights.claim: Another round of war on top of the Saudi-Houthi war would leave damage to infrastructure and to importers' confidence that markets are likely to carry for a generation.
insights.speaker: Amir Handjani
insights.so_what: Long-horizon energy allocation decisions may tilt durably away from Gulf supply.

themes.theme: Post-midterm escalation risk vs negotiated settlement

insights.claim: U.S. and Israeli planners have drawn up options for a short, intensive campaign against Iran's nuclear, missile, drone and energy infrastructure after the Nov. 3 midterms, per the New York Times, though Trump has not approved it; the WSJ reported Washington told Gulf governments to prepare.
insights.speaker: Amir Handjani
insights.so_what: A near-term escalation catalyst sits just after the U.S. midterms.
insights.locator: U.S. and Israeli planners have drawn

insights.claim: Iranian officials have named Saudi oil facilities, Gulf data centers and undersea cables as targets in any renewed round.
insights.speaker: Amir Handjani
insights.so_what: Retaliation risk extends beyond energy to Gulf digital infrastructure and AI/data center buildouts.
insights.quote: Iranian officials have responded by naming Saudi oil facilities, Gulf data centers, and undersea cables as targets.
insights.locator: U.S. and Israeli planners have drawn

insights.claim: Qatari mediators delivered a draft agreement to Tehran on Oct. 25 reportedly setting out a seven-day sequence of reciprocal confidence-building steps backed by guarantor states; Washington has shifted from demanding an end to enrichment to a 'meaningful' reduction, while Tehran prioritizes relief from the U.S. naval blockade and oil sanctions.
insights.speaker: Amir Handjani
insights.so_what: A visible diplomatic off-ramp creates two-sided risk for oil risk premia.

insights.claim: U.S. military costs of the war reached $47.1 billion by mid-October per CENTCOM, $29 billion of it for replacing expended munitions.
insights.speaker: Amir Handjani
insights.so_what: Heavy munitions replenishment spending supports defense contractor demand and adds fiscal pressure.

insights.claim: The author argues a short campaign would not repair Ras Laffan or restore Saudi spare capacity and would invite exactly the retaliation air defenses cannot fully stop, making negotiated concessions cheaper than another round.
insights.speaker: Amir Handjani
insights.so_what: From an energy-market view, escalation has asymmetric downside versus a deal.
